---
title: "Quiz: bleed-through and compensation"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A pixel with dye amounts $\mathbf a$ records $\mathbf y = M\mathbf a$ (rows = channels, columns = dyes); with two dyes and each column scaled to its own channel, $M = S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & s_{12} \\ s_{21} & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

---

**Q1.** Why does a green dye show up in an orange channel, but an orange dye hardly in a green channel?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Look at the shape of an emission spectrum on both sides of its peak.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Emission spectra have a long tail towards **longer** wavelengths (the red side) and fall off quickly on the short side. The green dye's red tail reaches into the orange channel's band; the orange dye emits almost nothing at green wavelengths. So $s_{21}$ (green into orange) is typically 10–30 %, $s_{12}$ only a few percent.
:::

---

**Q2.** What does the second column of $M$ tell you?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Multiply $M$ by $(0, 1)^\top$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$M(0, 1)^\top$ is the second column: what the channels record for one unit of dye 2 and nothing else. It is dye 2 "as the channels see it": its emission spectrum seen through the filters.
:::

---

**Q3.** With $S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0.3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, a pixel records $(500, 400)$. How much of dye 2 does it contain?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Channel 1 sees only dye 1 here.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Channel 1 sees only dye 1, so $a_1 = 500$. Channel 2 sees $0.3 \cdot 500 = 150$ from dye 1, so $a_2 = 400 - 150 = 250$. (This is $S^{-1}\mathbf y$ with $S^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -0.3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.)
:::

---

**Q4.** You compensate an image and the nucleus (only dye 1) now has clearly **negative** values in the dye-2 image. What went wrong, and in which direction should you change $s_{21}$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How much of channel 1 did you subtract from channel 2?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Over-compensation: you subtracted too much of channel 1 from channel 2, so $s_{21}$ is too large. Lower it until the nucleus sits at the background level and does not tilt with its own brightness. No dye emits negative light, so negative values are the sign of a mistake even without ground truth.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why should the background (dark offset) be subtracted before you estimate a spillover from a single-stained control?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The slope is fitted through the origin.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The model $y_2 = s_{21}\, y_1$ holds for the light from the dye. An offset adds a constant to both channels, a fake "component" with a flat spectrum; a line through the origin fitted to shifted points has the wrong slope (dim pixels are pulled most). After subtracting the offset, zero dye means zero signal.
:::

---

**Q6.** Two dyes give $S = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0.8 \\ 0.8 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Without computing the inverse: will compensation work well? What happens to the noise?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compute $\det S$, the area spanned by the columns.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\det S = 1 - 0.64 = 0.36$: the columns are fairly parallel. Compensation still gives the right values **on average**, but $S^{-1} = \frac{1}{0.36}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -0.8 \\ -0.8 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$ has entries near 2.8 and −2.2, so the noise of each pixel is amplified about two to three times. Better: dyes or filters that are further apart.
:::

---

**Q7.** Two proteins sit in different compartments, but Pearson's correlation between the two channels is 0.4. Give an explanation that has nothing to do with biology.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does bleed-through put into channel 2?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Bleed-through: channel 2 contains a fraction of dye 1's light, so wherever channel 1 is bright, channel 2 is a little bright too. Independent channels become correlated. Compensate first (in the demo $r$ drops from 0.33 to about 0).
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that compensating a dye-1-only pixel $\mathbf y = a(1, s)^\top$ with the guess $g$ (and $s_{12} = 0$) gives $\hat a_2 = (s - g)\,a$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$S_g^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -g & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$S_g^{-1}\mathbf y = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -g & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} a \\ s a \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} a \\ (s - g) a \end{pmatrix}$. Plotted against $\hat a_1 = a$, the population is a line with slope $s - g$: zero only for the right guess.
:::
